issues.item: Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings
issues.explanation: Avoiding religious spaces is not clearly linked to the indexed trauma of mugging/robbery, and no other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal item provides a plausible religious cue or meaning that would explain this highly specific avoidance.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: The threat profile centers on generalized hypervigilance after robbery, but specifically listening for someone entering the home implies a home-intrusion context that is unsupported by the trauma type and by the rest of the selected items; this makes the item hard to reconcile with the same indexed event.

vignette:
Leila, a 26-year-old non-binary veterinarian in a long-term relationship, had been working a late shift at a small animal clinic in a busy strip mall when the mugging happened. It was just after closing, and they were carrying the day’s deposits to their car in the rear parking lot when two men came up fast from the shadowed side of the building. One had a hand in his jacket and barked for Leila’s bag; the other stayed close enough that Leila could smell cigarette smoke and cheap cologne, a smell that still comes back with painful clarity when they think about it. Leila remembered the sound of their own voice turning thin and polite, offering the bag immediately, apologizing, trying not to anger anyone. They had gone rigidly compliant, fawning through the fear, because in that moment being agreeable felt safer than resisting. Even now, when they try to explain what happened, they lose the thread partway through and cannot finish the story cleanly; the memory seems to splinter as soon as they begin, and sometimes all they can get out is that it was “bad” before going silent. At other times the whole scene arrives without warning from something ordinary—a man’s shoes in a parking lot, the scrape of tires, a whiff of smoke near a clinic entrance—and in an instant the full memory is back, vivid and body-tight, as if the mugging is happening again.

Since then, Leila has come to believe that life has changed in a permanent and uglier way. They say they used to be a happy person, but now they feel miserable much of the time, and that misery has hardened into the conviction that they have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. They no longer trust other people in the way they used to; strangers feel unpredictable, and even familiar settings feel dangerous in a way they did not before. That belief has reshaped their days. Leila scans their surroundings constantly for signs of danger, checks behind them when walking from the clinic to the parking lot, and keeps one eye on reflections in shop windows or car mirrors. They are still on guard inside their own home, listening for footsteps in the hall and tense at every unexpected sound, as if danger could be waiting just beyond the door. The same fear has made going out increasingly difficult, and they have started turning down evening plans with friends and avoiding unnecessary trips after dark. At work, they now choose routes that let them see who is behind them, and they make a point of arriving and leaving at times when the lot is less empty.

The more Leila tries to stay safe, the more their world seems to shrink around the mugging. When they notice themselves scanning and checking, the memory can rush back with surprising force, bringing with it the smell, the parking lot, and the helplessness of that night. Once the memory appears, they quickly slip into old habits of trying to smooth everything over—being extra compliant with anyone who seems irritated, overexplaining themselves, apologizing too much, and avoiding any confrontation that might feel risky. Afterward, they judge themselves for these habits and feel even less like the person they used to be, as if the event has made them smaller and weaker than they can bear to admit. In those moments, the old thought returns that they cannot rely on other people anyway, and that only constant vigilance keeps them intact. That belief, in turn, keeps them scanning harder, checking more often, and withdrawing further from going out, which leaves more room for the memory to intrude and the sense of danger to deepen. By the time Leila sought help, their relationship had begun to feel the strain of how rarely they wanted to leave home in the evenings, and they were exhausted by the effort of seeming calm while remaining braced for the next threat. What brought them in now was the fear that this way of living would become permanent, and what they most hope for is some way to feel safe again without having to keep watch every second.
